newsitem.title: PANAMA: Few bold solutions at Central American summit.
newsitem.headline: Few bold solutions at Central American summit.

text.p: Central American heads of state wound down their 19th Presidential Summit on Saturday, drawing up some measures to boost trade but failing to agree on reforms to trim the region's institutions.
Specific plans to transform Central America into a powerful free trade zone failed to materialise and the final summit declaration made scant reference about this issue.

Instead, the one-day summit saw the revival of old tensions between the Central American countries -- still recovering from Cold-War era civil wars -- and prevented leaders from reaching a decision on slashing the size and cost of regional institutions.

The Central American Parliament (PARLACEN) and Central American Court of Justice (CJJ) came under the toughest scrutiny for their burden on a region of 32 million people where average per capita gross domestic product ranges from $481 in Nicaragua to $2,641 in Panama per year.

"We have moved towards an agreement about the institutional reforms of Central America to guarantee that the institutions of regional integration are functioning efficiently," Panama's President Ernesto Perez Balladares said in a speech to close the summit.

But the region's presidents failed to reach agreement on reducing the size of PARLACEN, seen as a burden on the region's budgets. President Perez Balladares said a commission would be set up to find ways of reforming the parliament.
Guatemala's President Alvaro Arzu had urged leaders at the opening of the summit to act with "firmness and boldness" to keep alive the process of regional integration.
These regional institutions, developed during the transition from civil wars to democracy in the early 1990s, have been lambasted as toothless and expensive talking-shops.
While officials privately acknowledged the summit had done little to resolve long-standing differences, their public statements were upbeat.

"We have taken advantage at this meeting to advance the consolidation of the Central American community. It is our wish to create an institutional framework which will unite us more, but respect the differences of each country," said the summit declaration signed by the six Central American presidents.

The presidents ratified a watered down version of a free-trade agreement between Central America and Panama, often considered the odd-man out in issues of regional integration. Panama is currently the only country that is not a member of the Central American Common Market.

The agreement will "initiate negotiations for a free-trade treaty" between Central America and Panama, but finance ministers at the summit said no date had been set for when the treaty would come into effect.

In preparatory talks on Friday, the region's foreign ministers agreed on a resolution to work together to combat money laundering. The presidents also signed a declaration which spelled out their dissatisfaction at U.S. plans to deport illegal immigrants back to Central America.

Attending the summit were Costa Rican President Jose Maria Figueres, Honduran President Carlos Roberto Reina, Nicaraguan President Alvaro Arzu, El Salvador's President Armando Calderon Sol, Guatemala's Arzu and Panama's Balladares.

Also attending as a guest was Dominican Republic President Lionel Fernandez, who wanted to expand his Caribbean island's commerce with Central America. Vice Prime Minister Dean Barrow, of English-speaking Belize, attended as an observer.
Fernandez said the Dominican Republic would host the next Central American Presidential Summit in November.
